title: Time, days & months
goal: Tell the time, name the days and months, and say when things happen — today, tomorrow, in the evening, on Friday.
intro:
Sindhi tells the time with **وڳو** (vaɠo, 'stroke, o'clock' — from the striking of a gong) and has handy words for quarter and half hours: **سوا** (savā, quarter past), **ساڍا** (sāḍhā, half past), **پوڻا** (pauṇā, quarter to), and the special **ڏيڍ** (1:30) and **اڍائي** (2:30).

Note that **ڪالهه** (kālha) is only 'yesterday' and **سڀاڻي** (subhāṇe) only 'tomorrow' — unlike Urdu *kal*, Sindhi keeps them apart.

phrases.en: What time is it? (lit. how many o'clocks are there)
It's half past four. (lit. half past four has become)
What time is the class? (lit. at how many o'clock)
Sorry I'm late. (lit. it became late)

phrases.native: مون وٽ وقت ناهي، مان جلدي ۾ آهيان.
phrases.roman: moṃ vaṭi vaqtu nāhe, māṃ jaldī meṃ āhiyāṃ.
phrases.en: I don't have time, I'm in a hurry.

grammar.title: Telling the time
grammar.body:
Ask **ڪيترا وڳا آهن؟** 'how many o'clocks are there?' Answer with number + **وڳا** (plural) + آهن — except for one o'clock: **هڪ وڳو آهي**.

**Quarters and halves** go in front of the hour:
سوا ٽي savā ṭe — 3:15 (quarter past three)
ساڍا ٽي sāḍhā ṭe — 3:30
پوڻا چار pauṇā chāri — 3:45 (quarter to four)
But 1:30 is **ڏيڍ** (ɗeḍhu) and 2:30 is **اڍائي** (aḍhāī) — never 'sāḍhā hiku/ɓa'.

For exact minutes, especially in cities, people usually say the time in Urdu or English ('das pandrah' or 'ten fifteen') — that's normal.

**At** a time uses an oblique form ending in **-īṃ** + **وڳي** (vaɠe): پنجين وڳي 'at five', ڏهين وڳي 'at ten' (but هڪ وڳي 'at one', ٻين وڳي 'at two', ٽين وڳي 'at three', چئين وڳي 'at four'), ڪيتري وڳي؟ 'at what time?'. Parts of the day take **جو** 'of': صبح جو 'in the morning', رات جو 'at night'.

examples.native: دڪان رات جو ڏهين وڳي بند ٿئي ٿو.
examples.roman: dukānu rāti jo ɗahīṃ vaɠe bandu thie tho.
examples.en: The shop closes at ten at night.

grammar.title: Days, months and time expressions
grammar.body:
With days, **تي** (te, 'on') is usually used: **سومر تي** 'on Monday', or just سومر ڏينهن 'Monday-day'. Time words like اڄ، سڀاڻي، ڪالهه، هاڻي need no postposition.

**'Next' and 'last'** are ايندڙ (endaṛu) and گذريل (guzriyalu); with a postposition (or as a time adverb) the noun goes oblique: ايندڙ هفتي 'next week', گذريل مهيني 'last month'.

**Months.** Everyday life uses the Western months, in Sindhi spelling: جنوري، فيبروري، مارچ، اپريل، مئي، جون، جولاءِ، آگسٽ، سيپٽمبر، آڪٽوبر، نومبر، ڊسمبر. The traditional Sindhi calendar — still used for festivals, farming and poetry — runs: چيٽ Cheṭ (March–April), وهاڱو, ڄيٺ, آکاڙ, سانوڻ, بڊو, اسو, ڪتي, ناهري, پوهه, مانگهه, ڦڳڻ. The Islamic months (رمضان، عيد…) set the religious calendar.

examples.native: اسين آچر تي آرام ڪريون ٿا.
examples.roman: asīṃ āchara te ārāmu karyūṃ thā.

examples.native: چيٽي چنڊ چيٽ جي مهيني ۾ ٿئي ٿو.
examples.roman: cheṭī chanḍu cheṭa jī mahīne meṃ thie tho.
examples.en: Cheti Chand falls in the month of Chet.

dialogue.title: Making a plan
dialogue.setting: Two friends, Sorath and Amar, arrange to visit the Sindh Museum in Hyderabad.

lines.speaker: Sorath
lines.en: Yes, Saturday. Shall we go to the museum?

lines.speaker: Sorath
lines.native: ڏهين وڳي؟ صبح جو گرمي گهٽ هوندي.
lines.roman: ɗahīṃ vaɠe? subuh jo garmī ghaṭu hundī.
lines.en: At ten? It'll be less hot in the morning.

lines.speaker: Amar
lines.native: ڏهين وڳي ڏاڍو جلدي آهي! ساڍا يارهن؟
lines.roman: ɗahīṃ vaɠe ɗāḍho jaldī āhe! sāḍhā yārahaṃ?
lines.en: Ten is too early! Half past eleven?

lines.speaker: Sorath
lines.native: چڱو، ساڍا يارهن. دير نه ڪر!
lines.roman: chaṅgo, sāḍhā yārahaṃ. dera na kar!
lines.en: OK, eleven thirty. Don't be late!

culture: **Cheti Chand** (چيٽي چنڊ), the first new moon of the month of Cheṭ (usually late March or early April), is the Sindhi New Year and the festival of **Jhulelal** (جهوليلال), the river-saint associated with the Indus, honoured especially by Hindu Sindhis in Sindh and India with processions, music and offerings to the water. In Pakistan the working week runs Monday to Saturday for many, with Sunday off; Friday midday is reserved for congregational prayers. Sindh also celebrates **Sindhi Culture Day** (Ajrak-Topi Day) on the first Sunday of December.
